questions.stem: Which analogy describes Data Generalisation versus Data Specialisation?
options: Encrypt versus decrypt
Backup versus restore
Read versus write
Zoom-out versus zoom-in, or less precise versus precise
Batch versus real-time
questions.explanation: Data Generalisation or Blurring and Specialisation are like zoom-out versus zoom-in, or precise versus less precise.

questions.stem: What does Data Generalisation do to data?
options: Summarises it in such a way that its usefulness remains intact
Deletes all personal information permanently
Splits each entity into several smaller entities
Encrypts it with a private key
Duplicates it across several servers
questions.explanation: Data Generalisation summarises data so that the usefulness of the data remains intact while the original values are not exposed.

options: Summarises several entities into one
Replaces values with dummy values
Divides an entity into multiple entities to further make sense of the data
Removes identifying columns
Converts data into age ranges
questions.explanation: Data Specialisation is the opposite of Data Generalisation: it divides an entity into multiple entities.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the example of Data Generalisation given in I Am Datapedia!?
options: Splitting an account table into current and savings account tables
Creating a summarised Person entity that hosts both Students and Patients details
Swapping ages between records
Masking a credit card number
Replacing a password with asterisks
questions.explanation: Students and Patients both have Name and Mobile number, so a summarised Person entity can hold both, with nobody able to identify any individual student or patient.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the example of Data Specialisation given in I Am Datapedia!?
options: Combining Students and Patients into a Person entity
Grouping ages into ranges such as 20-29
Hiding an email address
Merging two customer tables into one
Dividing an account table into separate current account and savings account tables
questions.explanation: An account table holding both current and savings details can be divided into a current account table and a savings account table, a concept close to Normalisation.

questions.stem: When individual ages are replaced by ranges such as 20-29 (2) and 30-39 (3), what is achieved?
options: The data becomes reversible to its original values
The data loses all analytical value
The essence of the data is maintained but the original data is not exposed
Each person can still be identified by exact age
The data is encrypted
questions.explanation: Data Generalisation distorts actual data to a level where it does not lose its originality; the essence is kept but the original values are hidden.

questions.stem: What is the limitation of Declarative Generalisation?
options: It can only be done on a small dataset, because the data is distorted manually
It cannot be applied to personal data
It requires a machine learning model
It is not accepted by regulatory bodies
It always removes the identifying columns
questions.explanation: In Declarative Generalisation data is manually distorted, so it is limited to small datasets.

options: Data is distorted by hand using manual queries
Data is deleted once it reaches an age threshold
Data is copied to a secure server
Data is split into multiple tables
Algorithms distort the data until it meets accepted standards
questions.explanation: In Automated Generalisation, algorithms are used to distort the data to the level of accepted standards.

questions.stem: What is a Quasi Identifier in Data Generalisation?
options: A single column such as ID that uniquely identifies an entity
A combination of multiple columns that together can identify an entity
A column that has been masked
A randomly generated token
A column defined by a regulatory body
questions.explanation: With a Quasi Identifier, multiple columns are combined to identify an entity, allowing generalisation to be achieved to an acceptable level.

questions.stem: Why might masking a single Direct Identifier such as Name fail to fully achieve Data Generalisation?
options: Because names cannot be masked
Because Direct Identifiers are never used for identification
Because masking always removes the whole record
Because a single identifier is not guaranteed to be unique, for example there can be several people named Hube in the same city or postcode
Because regulators forbid masking names
questions.explanation: A single identifier such as ID, Name or Email is not guaranteed to be unique, so masking it alone might not fulfil the requirement of generalisation.
